Notation: |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α; M_W(T) := T.massOn W; val : ↥U → ℝ^P is the inclusion; H := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d).
1. (Coordinates.) By the sibling covector_euclidean_equiv choose d and c : Covector (Euclid P) n ≃L[ℝ] H with |α| = ‖c α‖. Thus |·| is a norm on covectors, and c, c⁻¹ are continuous linear.
2. (Extension.) By the sibling testform_extension (with P, n, U, T, d, c and the hypotheses) there is a linear L : C_c(U, H) → ℝ with (i) L(g) = T(ω) whenever g(x) = c(ω(x)) for all x ∈ U, and (ii) local boundedness on compact subsets of ↥U.

Apply the sibling vector_riesz to X := ↥U, d and L; its hypothesis is (ii). This gives a measure μ₀ on ↥U, finite on compact sets, and a measurable ν : ↥U → H, integrable on compact sets, with L(g) = ∫ ⟨g(x), ν(x)⟩ dμ₀(x) for all g ∈ C_c(U, H).
4. (Normalization and definitions.)
 - ρ(x) := ‖ν(x)‖ and ν̂(x) := ρ(x)⁻¹•ν(x), with 0⁻¹ = 0. Both are measurable, ν(x) = ρ(x)•ν̂(x) for all x, ‖ν̂(x)‖ ≤ 1, and ‖ν̂(x)‖ = 1 when ρ(x) ≠ 0.
 - μ₁ := μ₀.withDensity (x ↦ ofReal ρ(x)) on ↥U, and μ := μ₁.map val. Since U is open, hence measurable, val is a measurable embedding. So μ(A) = μ₁(val⁻¹A) for measurable A, and ∫ F dμ = ∫ F(val x) dμ₁(x) (MeasurableEmbedding.integral_map).
 - ν̂_e : ℝ^P → H is ν̂(⟨y, h⟩) for y ∈ U and 0 for y ∉ U. It is measurable, being measurable on the measurable set U and constant on Uᶜ.
 - ξ(y) := (innerSL ℝ (ν̂_e y)).comp c, so ξ(y)(α) = ⟨ν̂_e(y), c α⟩ and ξ(y) = 0 for y ∉ U.
 - β(y) := c⁻¹(ν̂_e(y)).
5. (Property 1.) μ(Uᶜ) = μ₁(val⁻¹(Uᶜ)) = μ₁(∅) = 0.
6. (Property 2.) Let K ⊆ U be compact. val⁻¹(K) is compact in ↥U, because val is an embedding and K ⊆ range val (Topology.IsInducing.isCompact_preimage_iff). So μ(K) = μ₁(val⁻¹K) = ∫⁻_{val⁻¹K} ofReal ρ dμ₀ < ∞, since ν is integrable on val⁻¹K.
7. (Properties 4 and 5.) The map Φ : H → MultiVector P n, Φ(v) := (innerSL ℝ v).comp c, is continuous linear, and ξ = Φ ∘ ν̂_e. ν̂_e is measurable into the second-countable space H, hence strongly measurable. So ξ is strongly measurable, in particular AEStronglyMeasurable for μ. For every y and α, |ξ(y)(α)| = |⟨ν̂_e(y), c α⟩| ≤ ‖ν̂_e(y)‖·‖c α‖ ≤ |α| (Cauchy–Schwarz). Likewise β = c⁻¹ ∘ ν̂_e is strongly measurable, and |β(y)| = ‖ν̂_e(y)‖ ≤ 1.
8. (Property 6.) Let ω ∈ TestFormOn U n and g_ω : ↥U → H, g_ω(x) := c(ω(val x)). g_ω is continuous. Its support is contained in val⁻¹(tsupport ω), which is compact because tsupport ω is a compact subset of U = range val. Hence g_ω ∈ C_c(U, H), and by step 2(i), T(ω) = L(g_ω). By step 3:
 L(g_ω) = ∫ ⟨c(ω x), ν x⟩ dμ₀
 = ∫ ρ(x)⟨ν̂(x), c(ω x)⟩ dμ₀(x)   (ν = ρ•ν̂, and the inner product is symmetric)
 = ∫ ⟨ν̂(x), c(ω x)⟩ dμ₁(x)   (integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul, with (ofReal ρ).toReal = ρ)
 = ∫ ξ(val x)(ω(val x)) dμ₁(x)
 = ∫ ξ(y)(ω y) dμ(y).
9. (μ-a.e. normalization.) The set Z := Uᶜ ∪ val''{x : ρ x = 0} is measurable, and μ(Z) ≤ μ(Uᶜ) + μ₁({ρ = 0}) = 0 + ∫⁻_{ρ=0} ofReal ρ dμ₀ = 0. For y = val x ∉ Z, ξ(y)(β y) = ⟨ν̂ x, c(c⁻¹(ν̂ x))⟩ = ‖ν̂ x‖² = 1. So ξ(y)(β(y)) = 1 for μ-a.e. y.
10. (Property 3, upper bound.) Let W be open and ω ∈ massAdmissibleOn U n W. If μ(W) = ∞ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise y ↦ ξ(y)(ω y) vanishes off W (ω(y) = 0 for y ∉ tsupport ω), and |ξ(y)(ω y)| ≤ |ω y| ≤ 1. By step 8, T(ω) = ∫_W ξ(ω) dμ ≤ (μ W).toReal, so ofReal(T ω) ≤ μ(W). Taking the supremum over ω, M_W(T) ≤ μ(W).
11. (Property 3, lower bound on relatively compact pieces.) Let W be open and W' an open set with W' ⊂⊂ U and W' ⊆ W.
 - ν' := μ.restrict W' is a finite measure (μ(W') ≤ μ(closure W') < ∞ by step 6) with ν'(W'ᶜ) = 0. β is integrable for ν', being strongly measurable and bounded, and |β| ≤ 1.

 - By step 8, since ω vanishes off W', T(ω) = ∫_{W'} ξ(ω) dμ = ∫_{W'} ξ(β) dμ + ∫_{W'} ξ(ω − β) dμ; both integrands are bounded on the finite-measure set W'. By step 9 the first integral is μ.real(W'). The second has absolute value ≤ ∫_{W'} |ω − β| dμ < ε, since |ξ(y)(α)| ≤ |α|.

The open set O is the increasing union of the open sets W'_j (j ≥ 1), where W'_j := ball(0, j) if O = ℝ^P, and W'_j := {y : ‖y‖ < j and infDist(y, Oᶜ) > 1/j} otherwise. The hypotheses are referred to as:
(B) the boundary mass is finite;
(1) μ(Uᶜ) = 0;
(2) μ(K) < ∞ for compact K ⊆ U;
(3) M_W(T) = μ(W) for open W;
(4) ξ is a.e.-strongly measurable;

1. (n = 0.) μHE[0] = μH[0] (Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_zero) and μH[0]({x}) = 1 (Measure.hausdorffMeasure_zero_singleton). If x ∈ E then 1 = μH[0]({x}) ≤ μH[0](E) = 0, which is impossible. So E = ∅ and μ(E) = 0. From now on n = m + 1. Then boundaryMassOn T W = T.boundary.massOn W =: M_W(∂T) by definition, and ∂T := T.boundary ∈ 𝒟_m(U).
2. (Compact null sets: setup.) Let C ⊆ U be compact with Hⁿ(C) = 0; we show μ(C) = 0. This is clear if C = ∅. Otherwise choose δ > 0 with cthickening δ C ⊆ U (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open) and let W := thickening(δ/2) C. W is open, C ⊆ W, and closure W ⊆ cthickening(δ/2) C, which is compact and contained in U. So W ⊂⊂ U and W ⊆ U. Then μ(W) ≤ μ(closure W) < ∞ by (2), M_W(T) = μ(W) < ∞ by (3), and M_W(∂T) < ∞ by (B).
3. (Projection of C.) Fix a strictly increasing I and an n-covector θ with θ(v) = det(Matrix.of fun k j => v j (I k)) for all v. Write q := q_I. q is linear and 1-Lipschitz, since ‖q x‖² = Σ_k x(I k)² ≤ Σ_l x(l)² = ‖x‖² for injective I. So N := q(C) is compact. On both ℝ^P and ℝⁿ, μHE[n] = c_n•μH[n] with the same constant c_n ≠ 0 (Measure.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_def, addHaarScalarFactor_volume_hausdorffMeasure_ne_zero). Hence μH[n](C) = 0. LipschitzOnWith.hausdorffMeasure_image_le (with constant 1) gives μH[n](N) ≤ μH[n](C) = 0. Hence μHE[n](N) = 0, and volume(N) = 0 by EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume.
4. (Divergence bound.) Let b : ℝ^P → ℝ be C^∞ with compact support and tsupport b ⊆ W.

Here div g(y) := LinearMap.trace ℝ (Euclid n) (fderiv ℝ g y). Put Λ_b := K_b·(M_W(∂T).toReal + M_W(T).toReal).
 - Let g be C^∞ with compact support and ‖g‖ ≤ 1, and take η, ζ as above. Since tsupport b ⊆ W ⊆ U, they define η' ∈ TestFormOn U m and ζ' ∈ TestFormOn U n. Let ω_g := exteriorDerivativeTestOn U m η' − ζ' ∈ TestFormOn U n. Its underlying form is x ↦ (b(x)·div g(q x))•θ.

So the sibling eval_mass_bound, applied to ∂T with W, η', r = K_b and to T with W, ζ', r = K_b, gives |∂T(η')| ≤ K_b·M_W(∂T).toReal and |T(ζ')| ≤ K_b·M_W(T).toReal. Hence |T(ω_g)| ≤ Λ_b.

 - X := ℝ^P and ν := μ.restrict W, which is finite by step 2;
 - q, which is continuous, hence measurable;
 - h := h_b, which is a.e.-strongly measurable by (4) (evaluation at θ is continuous linear) and bounded by sup|b|·|θ| by (5), hence integrable for the finite measure ν;

 It gives ∫_{q⁻¹(N)} b(x)ξ(x)(θ) d(μ.restrict W)(x) = 0.
6. (Localization.) Let f := indicator(q⁻¹(N)) (x ↦ ξ(x)(θ)). f is a.e.-strongly measurable and bounded by |θ|, hence locally integrable on W for μ, because μ is finite on compact subsets of W ⊆ U by (2). For every C^∞ compactly supported b with tsupport b ⊆ W, ∫ b(x)·f(x) dμ = ∫_W b·f dμ (b vanishes off W) = ∫_{q⁻¹(N)} b(x)ξ(x)(θ) d(μ.restrict W) = 0 by step 5. By IsOpen.ae_eq_zero_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq_zero (W open), f(x) = 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ W. For x ∈ C we have x ∈ W and q(x) ∈ N, so f(x) = ξ(x)(θ). Hence ξ(x)(θ) = 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ C.
7. (ξ = 0 a.e. on C.) For each strictly increasing I fix θ_I with the determinant formula (sibling coordinate_covectors, part (a)). Any θ with the same formula equals θ_I, since they agree on every v. Since Fin n → Fin P is finite, step 6 and ae_all_iff give: for μ-a.e. x ∈ C, ξ(x)(θ) = 0 for every strictly increasing I and every θ with the determinant formula for I. By part (b) of coordinate_covectors, ξ(x) = 0 for μ-a.e. x ∈ C.
8. (μ(C) = 0.) Let ω ∈ massAdmissibleOn U n W. The function y ↦ ξ(y)(ω y) vanishes outside W (ω(y) = 0 off tsupport ω ⊆ W), vanishes μ-a.e. on C (step 7), and is bounded by |ω(y)| ≤ 1 (by (5)). Hence by (6), T(ω) = ∫_{W∖C} ξ(ω) dμ ≤ μ(W∖C), which is finite, so ofReal(T ω) ≤ μ(W∖C). Taking the supremum, μ(W) = M_W(T) ≤ μ(W∖C) = μ(W) − μ(C); here C is closed, hence measurable, and μ(C) ≤ μ(W) < ∞. Thus μ(C) = 0.
9. (General E.)
 - Let E ⊆ ℝ^P with Hⁿ(E) = 0, and choose a measurable E' ⊇ E with Hⁿ(E') = 0 (exists_measurable_superset_of_null).
 - Write U = ⋃_j K_j with K_j compact: since U is open, take K_j := closedBall(0, j) if U = ℝ^P and K_j := {x : ‖x‖ ≤ j, infDist(x, Uᶜ) ≥ 1/j} otherwise.
 - Fix j. μ_j := μ.restrict K_j is finite by (2), hence locally finite and regular on ℝ^P (Measure.Regular.of_sigmaCompactSpace_of_isLocallyFiniteMeasure). So it is inner regular by compact sets on measurable sets of finite measure (MeasurableSet.exists_lt_isCompact_of_ne_top).
 - Suppose μ_j(E') > 0. Then there is a compact C ⊆ E' with μ_j(C) > 0. C ∩ K_j is a compact subset of U with Hⁿ(C ∩ K_j) ≤ Hⁿ(E') = 0, so μ(C ∩ K_j) = 0 by step 8, contradicting μ_j(C) = μ(C ∩ K_j) > 0.
 - Hence μ(E' ∩ K_j) = μ_j(E') = 0 for every j, and μ(E) ≤ μ(E') ≤ μ(Uᶜ) + Σ_j μ(E' ∩ K_j) = 0 by (1).

By the Alaoglu theorem there is a subsequence ... Notation: for r > 0 and A ⊆ ℝ^P, thickening(r, A) := {x : ∃ y ∈ A, |x − y| < r}, an open set, with thickening(r, ∅) = ∅.

1. Compact exhaustion. For m ∈ ℕ let K_m := closedBall(0, m) ∖ thickening((m+1)⁻¹, ℝ^P ∖ U). (a) K_m is compact: it is the intersection of a closed ball with the complement of an open set, hence closed and bounded in ℝ^P. (b) K_m ⊆ U: if x ∈ K_m and x ∉ U, then x ∈ ℝ^P ∖ U ⊆ thickening((m+1)⁻¹, ℝ^P ∖ U), contradicting x ∈ K_m. (c) Every compact C ⊆ U lies in some K_m: by Mathlib IsCompact.exists_thickening_subset_open there is δ > 0 with thickening(δ, C) ⊆ U, and C ⊆ closedBall(0, R) for some R ≥ 0 (C is bounded). Choose m ∈ ℕ with m ≥ R and (m+1)⁻¹ ≤ δ. For x ∈ C we have |x| ≤ m, and if some y ∉ U had |x − y| < (m+1)⁻¹ ≤ δ then y ∈ thickening(δ, C) ⊆ U, a contradiction; hence x ∈ K_m. (No case distinction is needed when U = ℝ^P: then the thickening of ∅ is ∅ and K_m = closedBall(0, m).)

2. Good subsequences. Call a strictly increasing ψ : ℕ → ℕ m-good if for every continuous f : ℝ^P → ℝ with tsupport f ⊆ K_m there is c ∈ ℝ with ∫ f dμ_{ψ(j)} → c as j → ∞. If ψ is m-good and τ : ℕ → ℕ is strictly increasing, then ψ ∘ τ is m-good, since τ(j) → ∞ and a subsequence of a convergent sequence converges to the same limit.

3. Claim A (one compact piece): for every m ∈ ℕ and every strictly increasing ψ there is a strictly increasing θ such that ψ ∘ θ is m-good. Proof. Let X := K_m (subtype) with the subspace topology and subspace σ-algebra, and ι : X → ℝ^P the inclusion. X is a compact (isCompact_iff_compactSpace) metrizable space, its σ-algebra is its Borel σ-algebra (Mathlib instance Subtype.borelSpace), and ι is a measurable embedding because K_m is closed, hence Borel (MeasurableEmbedding.subtype_coe). For j ∈ ℕ let λ_j := Measure.comap ι μ_{ψ(j)}, so λ_j(A) = μ_{ψ(j)}(ι(A)) for measurable A ⊆ X. For every compact A ⊆ X, λ_j(A) ≤ λ_j(X) = μ_{ψ(j)}(K_m) ≤ sup_i μ_i(K_m), and sup_i μ_i(K_m) < ∞ by the hypothesis applied to the compact set K_m ⊆ U; hence (⨆_j λ_j(A)) < ∞. Therefore SimonGMT Chapter01 simon_theorem_4_16_compact_metrizable (hypotheses: X compact, metrizable, Borel, and (⨆_j λ_j(A)) < ∞ for every compact A ⊆ X; no nonemptiness assumption) yields a strictly increasing θ and a measure ν on X with ∫ h dλ_{θ(j)} → ∫ h dν for every h ∈ C_c(X, ℝ). Now let f : ℝ^P → ℝ be continuous with tsupport f ⊆ K_m and put h := f ∘ ι. Then h is continuous on the compact space X, so h ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) (HasCompactSupport.of_compactSpace). For every measure ρ on ℝ^P, f(x) = 0 for x ∉ K_m (such x are not in tsupport f), so ∫ f dρ = ∫_{K_m} f dρ (setIntegral_eq_integral_of_forall_compl_eq_zero) = ∫_X h d(Measure.comap ι ρ) (integral_subtype_comap, K_m measurable). Taking ρ := μ_{ψ(θ(j))} gives ∫ f dμ_{ψ(θ(j))} = ∫ h dλ_{θ(j)} → ∫ h dν. Hence ψ ∘ θ is m-good.

4. Diagonal construction. Choose strictly increasing maps θ_m, ψ_m recursively: θ_0 is given by Claim A for the index 0 and ψ = id, and ψ_0 := θ_0; for m ≥ 0, θ_{m+1} is given by Claim A for the index m+1 and ψ = ψ_m, and ψ_{m+1} := ψ_m ∘ θ_{m+1}. By Claim A, ψ_m is m-good for every m. By induction on n ≥ m there is a strictly increasing τ_{m,n} with ψ_n = ψ_m ∘ τ_{m,n} (τ_{m,m} := id, τ_{m,n+1} := τ_{m,n} ∘ θ_{n+1}).

5. φ(j) := ψ_j(j) is strictly increasing. A strictly increasing map θ : ℕ → ℕ satisfies θ(n) ≥ n (StrictMono.id_le), so φ(j+1) = ψ_j(θ_{j+1}(j+1)) ≥ ψ_j(j+1) > ψ_j(j) = φ(j), because ψ_j is strictly increasing; strictMono_nat_of_lt_succ concludes.

6. Tails of φ are subsequences of ψ_m. Fix m and let σ(i) := τ_{m,i+m}(i+m), so that φ(i+m) = ψ_{i+m}(i+m) = ψ_m(σ(i)) for all i ∈ ℕ. σ is strictly increasing: ψ_m(σ(i)) = φ(i+m) < φ(i+m+1) = ψ_m(σ(i+1)) by step 5, and the strictly increasing ψ_m reflects <, so σ(i) < σ(i+1). Let f be continuous with tsupport f ⊆ K_m and let c be the limit of ∫ f dμ_{ψ_m(j)} (ψ_m is m-good). Since σ(i) → ∞, ∫ f dμ_{φ(i+m)} = ∫ f dμ_{ψ_m(σ(i))} → c as i → ∞, hence ∫ f dμ_{φ(j)} → c as j → ∞ (a shift of the index does not affect convergence, Filter.tendsto_add_atTop_iff_nat).

Every f ∈ C_c(U) has tsupport in some K_m, so ∫ f dμ_{φ(j)} converges.

0. Integrability. If f : ℝ^P → ℝ is continuous with compact support and S := tsupport f ⊆ U, then f is ν_j-integrable for every j: f is bounded (continuous with compact support), f = 0 off S, S is Borel, and ν_j(S) < ∞ because S is a compact subset of U.

1. The space Y. Let Y := U (subtype) with the subspace topology and subspace σ-algebra, and ι : Y → ℝ^P the inclusion. Y is Hausdorff and locally compact (an open subset of ℝ^P, IsOpen.locallyCompactSpace), its σ-algebra is its Borel σ-algebra (Subtype.borelSpace), and ι is an open topological embedding and a measurable embedding (U is open, hence Borel).

2. Extension by zero. For g ∈ C_c(Y, ℝ) define ĝ : ℝ^P → ℝ by ĝ(x) := g(x) for x ∈ U and ĝ(x) := 0 for x ∉ U (in Lean: Function.extend Subtype.val g 0). Then: (a) ĝ ∘ ι = g. (b) ĝ is continuous: at x ∈ U because U is an open neighbourhood of x on which ĝ agrees with the continuous function g; at x ∉ U because S_g := ι(tsupport g) is compact, hence closed, x ∉ S_g, and ĝ = 0 on the open neighbourhood ℝ^P ∖ S_g of x (HasCompactSupport.continuous_extend_zero). (c) tsupport ĝ ⊆ S_g, which is compact and contained in U; hence ĝ has compact support and tsupport ĝ ⊆ U (HasCompactSupport.tsupport_extend_zero_subset, HasCompactSupport.extend_zero). (d) g ↦ ĝ is ℝ-linear ((a g₁ + b g₂)^ = a ĝ₁ + b ĝ₂ pointwise) and order preserving (g ≥ 0 ⇒ ĝ ≥ 0).

3. The limit functional. For g ∈ C_c(Y, ℝ) let Λ(g) := lim_j ∫ ĝ dν_j, formally Λ(g) := limUnder atTop (j ↦ ∫ ĝ dν_j); by the hypothesis, which applies to ĝ by step 2(b),(c), the sequence converges, so ∫ ĝ dν_j → Λ(g) (tendsto_nhds_limUnder). Λ is linear: by step 0 every ĝ is ν_j-integrable, so ∫ (a ĝ₁ + b ĝ₂) dν_j = a ∫ ĝ₁ dν_j + b ∫ ĝ₂ dν_j for every j; the left side tends to Λ(a g₁ + b g₂) (as (a g₁ + b g₂)^ = a ĝ₁ + b ĝ₂) and the right side to a Λ(g₁) + b Λ(g₂), so the two agree by uniqueness of limits in ℝ (tendsto_nhds_unique). Λ is positive: if g ≥ 0 then ĝ ≥ 0, so ∫ ĝ dν_j ≥ 0 for all j and Λ(g) ≥ 0 (ge_of_tendsto'). Thus Λ is a positive linear functional on C_c(Y, ℝ) (PositiveLinearMap.mk₀).

4. Riesz–Markov–Kakutani. μ_Y := RealRMK.rieszMeasure Λ is a regular Borel measure on Y, in particular finite on every compact subset of Y, and ∫ g dμ_Y = Λ(g) for every g ∈ C_c(Y, ℝ) (RealRMK.integral_rieszMeasure).

5. The measure μ := Measure.map ι μ_Y.
(a) μ(ℝ^P ∖ U) = μ_Y(ι⁻¹(ℝ^P ∖ U)) = μ_Y(∅) = 0.
(b) If K ⊆ U is compact, then ι⁻¹(K) is compact in Y (ι is an embedding and K ⊆ ι(Y)), so μ(K) = μ_Y(ι⁻¹(K)) < ∞ by step 4.
(c) Let f : ℝ^P → ℝ be continuous with compact support and tsupport f ⊆ U. Then g := f ∘ ι is continuous on Y and tsupport g ⊆ ι⁻¹(tsupport f) (tsupport_comp_subset_preimage), a compact subset of Y by (b)'s argument; hence g ∈ C_c(Y, ℝ). Moreover ĝ = f: for x ∈ U, ĝ(x) = g(x) = f(x); for x ∉ U, x ∉ tsupport f, so f(x) = 0 = ĝ(x). Therefore ∫ f dμ = ∫ f ∘ ι dμ_Y (MeasurableEmbedding.integral_map) = Λ(g) = lim_j ∫ ĝ dν_j = lim_j ∫ f dν_j, i.e. ∫ f dν_j → ∫ f dμ.
Together (a), (b), (c) prove the statement. ∎
proof_key_steps: Extension by zero identifies C_c(U, ℝ) on the subtype U with continuous compactly supported f on ℝ^P with tsupport f ⊆ U (HasCompactSupport.continuous_extend_zero).
Λ(g) := lim_j ∫ ĝ dν_j (limUnder) is a positive linear functional on C_c(U, ℝ); linearity uses ν_j-integrability from ν_j(K) < ∞ and uniqueness of limits.
RealRMK.rieszMeasure on the locally compact Hausdorff subtype U gives a regular μ_U with ∫ g dμ_U = Λ(g).
μ := push-forward of μ_U under Subtype.val: μ(Uᶜ) = 0, μ(K) < ∞ for compact K ⊆ U, and ∫ f dμ = Λ(f ∘ val) = lim_j ∫ f dν_j.

0. Integral-versus-measure comparisons. Let ρ be a Borel measure on ℝ^P and h : ℝ^P → ℝ continuous with 0 ≤ h ≤ 1 and compact support, with ρ(tsupport h) < ∞. Then h is ρ-integrable (bounded, zero off a set of finite measure) and ofReal(∫ h dρ) = ∫⁻ ofReal(h) dρ (ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal). Consequently: (i) if h = 1 on a closed set B, then ρ(B) ≤ ofReal(∫ h dρ), since 1_B ≤ ofReal ∘ h; (ii) if h = 0 off a Borel set V, then ofReal(∫ h dρ) ≤ ρ(V), since ofReal ∘ h ≤ 1_V. (Inequality (ii) holds even without integrability, because then ∫ h dρ = 0.) By hypothesis, ρ(tsupport h) < ∞ holds for ρ = ν_j (every j) and ρ = μ whenever tsupport h is a compact subset of U.

3. Compact subsets of open sets. Let G ⊆ U be open and C ⊆ G compact; we show μ(C) ≤ liminf_j ν_j(G). If C = ∅ this is trivial. Otherwise choose δ > 0 with cthickening(δ, C) ⊆ G (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open) and let h := h_{C,δ}: continuous, 0 ≤ h ≤ 1, h = 1 on C, tsupport h ⊆ cthickening(δ, C), a compact subset of G ⊆ U. By step 0(i) for ρ = μ, the hypothesis, and step 0(ii) for ρ = ν_j with V = G (h = 0 off G, G Borel):
μ(C) ≤ ofReal(∫ h dμ) = lim_j ofReal(∫ h dν_j) = liminf_j ofReal(∫ h dν_j) ≤ liminf_j ν_j(G).

Each C_n is closed and bounded, hence compact; C_n ⊆ G (a point of ℝ^P ∖ G lies in thickening((n+1)⁻¹, ℝ^P ∖ G)); C_n ⊆ C_{n+1}; and ⋃_n C_n = G: for x ∈ G pick r > 0 with ball(x, r) ⊆ G and n ≥ |x| with (n+1)⁻¹ ≤ r; any y with |x − y| < (n+1)⁻¹ lies in G, so x ∈ C_n. By continuity of μ from below along the increasing sequence C_n (tendsto_measure_iUnion_atTop), μ(G) = lim_n μ(C_n), and μ(C_n) ≤ liminf_j ν_j(G) for all n by step 3; hence μ(G) ≤ liminf_j ν_j(G) (le_of_tendsto'). ∎

Compact K: with h = 1 on K and tsupport h ⊆ cthickening(r, K), limsup_j ν_j(K) ≤ μ(cthickening(r, K)) → μ(K) (tendsto_measure_cthickening).
Compact C ⊆ open G: with h = 1 on C and tsupport h ⊆ G, μ(C) ≤ lim ofReal ∫ h dν_j ≤ liminf_j ν_j(G).

Put a_j := ∫_{f<t} g_j dμ_j = ∫ 1_{f<t} g_j dμ_j and a := ∫_{f<t} g dμ_X ({f < t} is open since f is continuous, hence Borel).

Mathlib exists_contDiff_support_eq_eq_one_iff, applied with smoothness order n := ⊤ (so that ContDiff ℝ ↑n is ContDiff ℝ ∞, the order required by IsSmoothForm), the open set s := ℝ^P ∖ C₂ and the closed set C₁ ⊆ s, gives χ : ℝ^P → ℝ of class C^∞ with values in [0, 1], support χ = ℝ^P ∖ C₂ (so χ = 0 on C₂) and χ = 1 on C₁. (Unlike the parent proof, χ need not have compact support: χω inherits compact support from ω.)

4. The test form ω_ε := χω, i.e. x ↦ χ(x)·ω(x). It is C^∞ (ContDiff.smul), its support is contained in support ω, so it has compact support (HasCompactSupport.smul_left), and tsupport ω_ε ⊆ tsupport ω ⊆ U (tsupport_smul_subset_right); so ω_ε ∈ 𝒟^k(U). Since ξ_j(x), ξ_X(x) are linear, ξ_j(x)(ω_ε(x)) = χ(x) g_j(x) and ξ_X(x)(ω_ε(x)) = χ(x) g(x); by the representation hypotheses X_j(ω_ε) = ∫ χ g_j dμ_j and X(ω_ε) = ∫ χ g dμ_X.

5. Error estimate. For x ∈ C: if f(x) ≤ t − ε then x ∈ C₁ and 1_{f<t}(x) − χ(x) = 1 − 1 = 0; if f(x) ≥ t then x ∈ C₂ and 1_{f<t}(x) − χ(x) = 0 − 0 = 0; and always |1_{f<t}(x) − χ(x)| ≤ 1. Off C, g_j = g = 0. Hence, with B'_ε := C ∩ {t − ε < f < t} ⊆ B_ε := C ∩ {t − ε ≤ f ≤ t}, we have |(1_{f<t} − χ) g_j| ≤ M·1_{B'_ε} μ_j-a.e. and |(1_{f<t} − χ) g| ≤ M·1_{B'_ε} μ_X-a.e., so
|a_j − X_j(ω_ε)| = |∫ (1_{f<t} − χ) g_j dμ_j| ≤ M μ_j(B_ε) and |a − X(ω_ε)| ≤ M μ_X(B'_ε)
(all these measures are finite, being at most μ_j(C) resp. μ_X(C); the inequalities are between real numbers).

6. Shrinking the band. The Borel sets B_{1/n} (n ≥ 1) decrease with ⋂_n B_{1/n} = C ∩ {f = t}, and μ(B_1) ≤ μ(C) < ∞, so μ(B_{1/n}) → μ(C ∩ {f = t}) ≤ μ{f = t} = 0 (continuity from above, tendsto_measure_iInter_atTop). Likewise B'_{1/n} decreases to ∅ and μ_X(B'_1) < ∞, so μ_X(B'_{1/n}) → 0.

7. Convergence. Let η > 0 and η' := η/(3(M+1)) > 0. By step 6 choose n ≥ 1 with μ(B_{1/n}) < η' and μ_X(B'_{1/n}) < η', and let ε := 1/n. B_ε is a closed subset of C, hence a compact subset of U, so by hypothesis limsup_j μ_j(B_ε) ≤ μ(B_ε) < η', whence μ_j(B_ε) < η' for all large j (eventually_lt_of_limsup_lt). By weak convergence X_j(ω_ε) → X(ω_ε), so |X_j(ω_ε) − X(ω_ε)| < η/3 for all large j. For all such j, step 5 gives
|a_j − a| ≤ |a_j − X_j(ω_ε)| + |X_j(ω_ε) − X(ω_ε)| + |X(ω_ε) − a| < Mη' + η/3 + Mη' < η.
As η > 0 was arbitrary, a_j → a, i.e. ∫_{f<t} ξ_j(ω) dμ_j → ∫_{f<t} ξ_X(ω) dμ_X. ∎

Source: Simon Ch. 6, 4.9-4.10 and the sentence between them (book/chapter-06.txt lines 1356-1377: “M_W(T⌞{f<t}) is increasing in t, hence is differentiable for L¹-a.e. t ∈ ℝ and ∫_a^b d/dt M_W(T⌞{f<t}) dt ≤ M_W(T⌞{a<f<b})”), and its use in the proof of 8.2, (2) (lines 2343-2347: “M(∂(T⌞B_r(ξ))) ≤ f'(r) for L¹-a.e. r > 0 ... f'(r) exists a.e. because f(r) is increasing”), as made precise in the parent proof, paragraph “Measurable majorant (MM)”, steps 12-16, with the Lean-level details filled in. Additions to the book (said explicitly): an arbitrary, possibly non-measurable G is handled by splitting only along the Borel strip {t − h < f < t}; the sequence version (liminf over j, Fatou's lemma) is the form needed in Remark 8.3(1) (“for some subsequence {j'}”, lines 2314-2316). Lean note: MonotoneOn.intervalIntegrable_deriv and MonotoneOn.intervalIntegral_deriv_mem_uIcc live in Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.IntervalIntegral.DerivIntegrable, which the frozen contract does not import; add `import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.IntervalIntegral.DerivIntegrable` to GMT/Ch07/Submission.lean. Notation: A(s) := G ∩ {a < f < s} for s ∈ ℝ (increasing in s, A(s) = ∅ for s ≤ a) and S_j(t, h) := μ_j(G ∩ {t − h < f < t}).

1. Trivial case. If b ≤ a then (a, b) = ∅: g := 0 is measurable, the a.e. statement is vacuous and ∫⁻_∅ 0 = 0 ≤ L·liminf_j μ_j(G ∩ {a < f < b}). Assume a < b from now on.

2. Distribution functions. For j ∈ ℕ define F_j : ℝ → ℝ, F_j(s) := (μ_j(A(min(s, b)))).toReal. Since A(min(s, b)) ⊆ A(b) = G ∩ {a < f < b}, which has finite μ_j-measure, s ↦ μ_j(A(min(s, b))) is nondecreasing with finite values; hence F_j is monotone (ENNReal.toReal_mono), F_j ≥ 0, ofReal(F_j(s)) = μ_j(A(min(s, b))), F_j(a) = μ_j(∅).toReal = 0 and F_j(b) = μ_j(G ∩ {a < f < b}).toReal.

3. Slice estimate: for t ∈ (a, b) and 0 < h < t − a, S_j(t, h) ≤ ofReal(F_j(t) − F_j(t − h)). Proof: S := {t − h < f < t} is open (f continuous), hence Borel, so for the arbitrary set E := A(t), μ_j(E) = μ_j(E ∩ S) + μ_j(E ∖ S) (measure_inter_add_sdiff). Since t − h > a, E ∩ S = G ∩ {t − h < f < t}, and E ∖ S ⊇ A(t − h). As t < b and t − h < b, μ_j(E) = ofReal(F_j(t)) and μ_j(A(t − h)) = ofReal(F_j(t − h)), all finite. Hence S_j(t, h) + ofReal(F_j(t − h)) ≤ ofReal(F_j(t)), so S_j(t, h) ≤ ofReal(F_j(t)) − ofReal(F_j(t − h)) = ofReal(F_j(t) − F_j(t − h)) (ENNReal.ofReal_sub, F_j(t − h) ≥ 0).

4. Bound at differentiability points. Let t ∈ (a, b) be a point where F_j is differentiable, with derivative deriv F_j t. The left difference quotients converge: h⁻¹(F_j(t) − F_j(t − h)) → deriv F_j t as h → 0, h > 0 (HasDerivAt.tendsto_slope_zero_left after the substitution h ↦ −h, or hasDerivAt_iff_tendsto_slope). For 0 < h < t − a, step 3 and ENNReal.ofReal_mul (h⁻¹ ≥ 0) give ofReal(h⁻¹)·S_j(t, h) ≤ ofReal(h⁻¹(F_j(t) − F_j(t − h))), and the right-hand side tends to ofReal(deriv F_j t) as h ↓ 0 (continuity of ofReal). The inequality holds on the set (0, t − a), which belongs to the filter 𝓝[>] 0, and this filter is nontrivial; hence liminf_{h↓0} ofReal(h⁻¹)·S_j(t, h) ≤ ofReal(deriv F_j t) (liminf_le_liminf and Tendsto.liminf_eq). By the hypothesis on Z_j and monotonicity of multiplication by L: Z_j(t) ≤ L·ofReal(deriv F_j t).

5. Exceptional null set. Each F_j is monotone, hence differentiable at L¹-a.e. t (Monotone.ae_differentiableAt); as ℕ is countable, for L¹-a.e. t every F_j is differentiable at t (ae_all_iff).

6. Definition and measurability of g. Let d_j(t) := ofReal(deriv F_j t) and g(t) := L·liminf_j d_j(t). deriv F_j is measurable (measurable_deriv), so each d_j is measurable, liminf_j d_j is measurable (Measurable.liminf), and g is measurable (Measurable.const_mul).

7. The a.e. bound. Let t ∈ (a, b) lie in the full-measure set of step 5. By step 4, Z_j(t) ≤ L·d_j(t) for every j, hence liminf_j Z_j(t) ≤ liminf_j (L·d_j(t)) = L·liminf_j d_j(t) = g(t), where the equality is ENNReal.liminf_const_mul_of_ne_top (L ≠ ∞).

8. Integral bound for one j. deriv F_j ≥ 0 everywhere (Monotone.deriv_nonneg). F_j is monotone on [a, b], so deriv F_j is interval integrable on [a, b] (MonotoneOn.intervalIntegrable_deriv) and ∫_a^b deriv F_j ∈ [0, F_j(b) − F_j(a)] (MonotoneOn.intervalIntegral_deriv_mem_uIcc; F_j(b) − F_j(a) ≥ 0, so the unordered interval is [0, F_j(b) − F_j(a)]). Since (a, b) and (a, b] differ by a null set (integral_Ioc_eq_integral_Ioo) and deriv F_j is nonnegative and integrable there, ∫⁻_{(a,b)} d_j = ofReal(∫_{(a,b)} deriv F_j) (ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal) = ofReal(∫_a^b deriv F_j) (intervalIntegral.integral_of_le) ≤ ofReal(F_j(b) − F_j(a)) = ofReal(F_j(b)) = μ_j(G ∩ {a < f < b}) (ENNReal.ofReal_toReal and the finiteness hypothesis).

9. Fatou. ∫⁻_{(a,b)} g = L·∫⁻_{(a,b)} liminf_j d_j (lintegral_const_mul, using step 6) ≤ L·liminf_j ∫⁻_{(a,b)} d_j (Fatou's lemma lintegral_liminf_le for the measurable d_j) ≤ L·liminf_j μ_j(G ∩ {a < f < b}) (step 8, liminf_le_liminf, and monotonicity of multiplication by L). Together with steps 6 and 7 this proves the statement. ∎
proof_key_steps: Trivial if b ≤ a; otherwise F_j(s) := μ_j(G ∩ {a < f < min(s,b)}).toReal is monotone with F_j(a) = 0 and F_j(b) = μ_j(G ∩ {a<f<b}).toReal.
Splitting E = G ∩ {a<f<t} along the Borel strip {t−h<f<t} (measure_inter_add_sdiff) gives μ_j(G ∩ {t−h<f<t}) ≤ F_j(t) − F_j(t−h).
Where all F_j are differentiable (a.e.), Z_j(t) ≤ L·ofReal(deriv F_j t); g := L·liminf_j ofReal(deriv F_j) is measurable and dominates liminf_j Z_j a.e. on (a,b).
∫⁻_{(a,b)} ofReal(deriv F_j) ≤ F_j(b) − F_j(a) ≤ μ_j(G ∩ {a<f<b}) (MonotoneOn.intervalIntegral_deriv_mem_uIcc); Fatou (lintegral_liminf_le) gives the integral bound.

By imrep_measure, for every IMRep R (in any set): (b) Hᵏ⌞M_R ≪ R.measure; (c) R.measure(A) = ∫_{M_R∩A} θ_R dHᵏ for every Borel A; (g) R.action ω = ∫ ξ_R(x)(ω(x)) dR.measure(x) for every k-form ω.
1. The case U = ∅. Then μ(ℝ^P) = μ(ℝ^P ∖ U) = 0, so X(ω) = ∫ ξ(ω) dμ = 0 for every ω. The IMRep in U with carrier ∅, multiplicity 0 and orientation 0 represents X: ∅ is Borel, ∅ ⊆ U, ∅ is countably k-rectifiable (SimonGMT countablyRectifiable_of_measure_zero), the multiplicity is measurable, the positivity condition is vacuous, every integral over ∅ is 0 (this gives local integrability and action 0 = X(ω)), and Hᵏ⌞∅ = 0, so the measurability and orientation conditions hold trivially. From now on U ≠ ∅.
2. Countable subcover. For each x ∈ U choose an open W_x ⊆ U with x ∈ W_x and an IMRep R_x in W_x as in the hypothesis. The open sets W_x (x ∈ U) cover U and ℝ^P is second countable, so there is a countable set T ⊆ U with ⋃_{x∈T} W_x = ⋃_{x∈U} W_x = U (Lindelöf; Mathlib TopologicalSpace.isOpen_iUnion_countable). T ≠ ∅ because U ≠ ∅, so T = {x_0, x_1, x_2, …} for a sequence (x_i)_{i∈ℕ} (Set.Countable.exists_eq_range; repetitions allowed). Write W_i := W_{x_i}, R_i := R_{x_i}, and M_i, θ_i, ξ_i for the carrier, multiplicity and orientation of R_i. Then each W_i is open, W_i ⊆ U, ⋃_i W_i = U, M_i ⊆ W_i, μ⌞W_i = R_i.measure, and ξ(y) = ξ_i(y) for μ-a.e. y ∈ W_i.
3. Disjoint pieces. Put A_i := W_i ∖ ⋃_{j<i} W_j (Mathlib disjointed). The A_i are Borel, pairwise disjoint, A_i ⊆ W_i, and ⋃_i A_i = ⋃_i W_i = U.
4. Glued data. Let M := ⋃_i (M_i ∩ A_i) and define θ : ℝ^P → ℕ by θ(y) := θ_i(y) if y ∈ A_i (the index i is unique) and θ(y) := 0 if y ∉ U (for instance θ(y) := θ_{n(y)}(y) with n(y) the least n such that y ∈ A_n, Nat.find, and θ(y) := 0 if there is no such n). Then: (i) M is Borel and M ⊆ U (M_i ⊆ W_i ⊆ U); since the A_i are pairwise disjoint, M ∩ A_i = M_i ∩ A_i for every i. (ii) θ is measurable: it takes values in the countable set ℕ, and for every m ∈ ℕ, θ⁻¹({m}) = ⋃_i (A_i ∩ θ_i⁻¹({m})) ∪ E_m with E_m := ℝ^P ∖ U if m = 0 and E_m := ∅ otherwise, a countable union of Borel sets (Mathlib measurable_to_countable'). (iii) θ = θ_i on A_i; in particular θ(y) = θ_i(y) ≥ 1 for y ∈ M_i ∩ A_i, so θ ≥ 1 on M. (iv) M is countably k-rectifiable: each M_i ∩ A_i ⊆ M_i is (SimonGMT CountablyRectifiable.mono), and so is the countable union (countablyRectifiable_iUnion).
5. The measure identity μ = (Hᵏ⌞M).withDensity θ. Let S be Borel. The sets S ∩ A_i are Borel and pairwise disjoint with union S ∩ U, and μ(ℝ^P ∖ U) = 0. Since S ∩ A_i ⊆ W_i and μ⌞W_i = R_i.measure, μ(S ∩ A_i) = μ(S ∩ A_i ∩ W_i) = R_i.measure(S ∩ A_i). 1. Restrictions. For every Borel E ⊆ B, μ₁⌞E = (μ₁⌞B)⌞E = ν⌞E and μ₂⌞E = (μ₂⌞B)⌞E = ν⌞E (Mathlib Measure.restrict_restrict_of_subset). For compact K ⊆ B, ν(K) = μ₁(K ∩ B) = μ₁(K) < ∞ by (i).

Since K is compact and B is open, there is δ > 0 with cthickening δ K ⊆ B (Mathlib IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open), and cthickening δ K is compact (IsCompact.cthickening; ℝ^P is proper). 5. Set integrals over Borel subsets of K. Let E ⊆ K be Borel. For y ∈ E, ξ_i(y)(ω(y)) = ξ_i(y)(α) = f_i^α(y), so the set integrals over E of ξ_i(ω) and of f_i^α coincide (setIntegral_congr_fun, E measurable). Using (v) and step 1 (E ⊆ K ⊆ B): ∫_E f₁^α dν = ∫_E f₁^α dμ₁ = ∫_E ξ₁(ω) dμ₁ = ∫_E ξ₂(ω) dμ₂ = ∫_E f₂^α dμ₂ = ∫_E f₂^α dν.
6. Equality a.e. on K. Let ν_K := ν⌞K, a finite measure by step 1. For every Borel s ⊆ ℝ^P, ν_K⌞s = ν⌞(s ∩ K) (Measure.restrict_restrict), and s ∩ K is a Borel subset of K, so by step 5, ∫_s f₁^α dν_K = ∫_{s∩K} f₁^α dν = ∫_{s∩K} f₂^α dν = ∫_s f₂^α dν_K. For j ∈ ℕ let K_j := B̄_j(0) ∖ T_j, where B̄_j(0) is the closed ball of radius j about 0 and T_j := {y : dist(y, z) < 1/(j+1) for some z ∈ ℝ^P ∖ B} is the open 1/(j+1)-neighbourhood of ℝ^P ∖ B (Mathlib thickening; T_j = ∅ if B = ℝ^P). Each K_j is a closed subset of a compact ball, hence compact; K_j ⊆ B, because every point of ℝ^P ∖ B lies in T_j; and ⋃_j K_j = B: a point y ∈ B is not in the closed set ℝ^P ∖ B, which is the intersection of its open δ-neighbourhoods (δ > 0), so y is outside the δ-neighbourhood for some δ > 0, and then y ∈ K_j for every j with j ≥ |y| and 1/(j+1) ≤ δ. Moreover ν(ℝ^P ∖ B) = 0, so ν-a.e. y lies in B and hence in some K_j. Therefore ξ₁(y)(α) = ξ₂(y)(α) for ν-a.e. y, for each fixed α ∈ Λ^k.

Write d(x) := inf{|x − y| : y ∈ ℝ^P ∖ O} ∈ [0, ∞] for the distance from x to ℝ^P ∖ O, with d(x) := +∞ for every x when O = ℝ^P (the infimum over the empty set). d is continuous as a map to [0, ∞] (it is 1-Lipschitz when ℝ^P ∖ O ≠ ∅ and constant otherwise), and d(x) = 0 for every x ∈ ℝ^P ∖ O.
1. (Exhaustion.) For i ∈ ℕ put O_i := {x ∈ ℝ^P : |x| < i and d(x) > 1/(i+1)}. (a) Each O_i is open: it is the intersection of the sets {|x| < i} and {d(x) > 1/(i+1)}, which are open by continuity of |·| and of d. (b) The set F_i := {x : |x| ≤ i and d(x) ≥ 1/(i+1)} is closed and contains O_i, so closure(O_i) ⊆ F_i. If x ∉ O, then d(x) = 0 < 1/(i+1), so x ∉ F_i; hence closure(O_i) ⊆ F_i ⊆ O. (c) closure(O_i) is closed and contained in the closed ball of radius i about 0, hence compact (Heine–Borel). (d) O_i ⊆ O_j whenever i ≤ j, since then |x| < i ≤ j and 1/(j+1) ≤ 1/(i+1). (e) ⋃_i O_i = O. Indeed O_i ⊆ closure(O_i) ⊆ O for every i. Conversely let x ∈ O. The set ℝ^P ∖ O is closed and does not contain x, so x is not in its closure and d(x) > 0. Choose an integer m ≥ 1 with 1/m < d(x) and an integer k > |x|, and put i := max(m, k). Then |x| < k ≤ i and 1/(i+1) < 1/m < d(x), so x ∈ O_i.
2. (Finiteness.) For each i, μ(O_i) ≤ μ(closure(O_i)) < ∞ by hypothesis, because closure(O_i) is a compact subset of O by step 1(b),(c). Since O_i is an open subset of O, ν(O_i) = μ(O_i) < ∞.
3. (Uniqueness on O_i.) Fix i and let μ_i := μ⌞O_i and ν_i := ν⌞O_i be the restricted measures, μ_i(B) = μ(B ∩ O_i) and ν_i(B) = ν(B ∩ O_i) for Borel B. By step 2 they are finite measures. For every open G ⊆ ℝ^P, the set G ∩ O_i is open and contained in O, so μ_i(G) = μ(G ∩ O_i) = ν(G ∩ O_i) = ν_i(G); in particular μ_i(ℝ^P) = ν_i(ℝ^P) (take G = ℝ^P). The family of open subsets of ℝ^P is closed under finite intersections (a π-system) and generates the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ^P. Two finite measures that have the same total mass and agree on a π-system generating the σ-algebra are equal (Dynkin's π–λ uniqueness theorem; Mathlib MeasureTheory.ext_of_generate_finite with isPiSystem_isOpen). Hence μ_i = ν_i.
4. (Continuity from below.) Let A ⊆ O be a Borel set. The sets A ∩ O_i increase with i by step 1(d), and ⋃_i (A ∩ O_i) = A ∩ ⋃_i O_i = A ∩ O = A by step 1(e). By continuity of measures from below, μ(A) = sup_i μ(A ∩ O_i) = sup_i μ_i(A) and ν(A) = sup_i ν(A ∩ O_i) = sup_i ν_i(A). By step 3, μ_i(A) = ν_i(A) for every i; therefore μ(A) = ν(A). ∎

μ(O_i) ≤ μ(closure O_i) < ∞ and ν(O_i) = μ(O_i), so μ⌞O_i and ν⌞O_i are finite measures.
μ⌞O_i and ν⌞O_i agree on every open G (G ∩ O_i is an open subset of O), including ℝ^P; open sets form a π-system generating the Borel σ-algebra, so μ⌞O_i = ν⌞O_i.
For Borel A ⊆ O, continuity from below along A ∩ O_i ↑ A gives μ(A) = sup_i μ(A ∩ O_i) = sup_i ν(A ∩ O_i) = ν(A).
